strengths: The core idea is useful and reasonably novel: distilling response-conditioned internal attention into a lightweight, partial-backbone RoI predictor avoids autoregressive localization at inference.

Results show large and consistent gains across document/OCR, general visual, and high-resolution benchmarks, including approximately 6.6–7.9 points average improvement on the five document/OCR tasks and 10–17 points on V-Star.
Evaluation covers four backbone configurations from two model families, providing meaningful evidence that the approach is not specific to one model size.
The component ablations support the practical value of selective label assignment, sink-token removal, masked upscaling, backbone depth, RPN depth, and training-set size.
Training requirements appear modest relative to full MLLM tuning, and the paper communicates the two-stage training and inference procedure clearly.
weaknesses: Model and method selection appear to use the same benchmarks reported as final results. Tables 4, 7, and 8 select backbone depth, RPN depth, and smoothing strategy using OCRBench, TextVQA, POPE, and V-Star scores, including an explicitly labeled OCRBench test split. Without a separate validation protocol, the headline evaluation is susceptible to benchmark overfitting.

The comparison set is narrow. Only S2 and ViCrop are evaluated against LLaVA, while DeepSeek-VL is compared only with its unmodified baseline. There are no comparisons with several relevant trained RoI, tiling, dynamic-resolution, or token-selection approaches discussed in the paper, nor matched-compute alternatives.

The efficiency evidence is incomplete: throughput is only relative, with no absolute latency, token counts, crop counts, FLOPs, memory usage, batch size, or measurement variance. The claim that the RoI prediction stage itself is 1.5× faster than ViCrop is not substantiated by a stage-level timing breakdown.

Important details needed for reproduction are missing, including the sink-norm threshold, Gaussian kernel parameters, inference threshold, crop resizing and padding rules, connected-component handling, maximum number of crops/tokens, and exact throughput protocol. The displayed code URL is also empty in the submitted manuscript.

The paper does not directly evaluate RoI quality using localization metrics, pseudo-label precision/recall, or an oracle-crop upper bound. Figure 3 and a small set of favorable qualitative examples are insufficient to establish that the RPN learns more precise localization rather than merely a crop policy that happens to improve downstream scores.

The theoretical appendix is largely tautological: it defines the target signal as E[A|X] and then observes that this conditional expectation has zero error relative to itself. It does not prove lower error relative to the latent foreground label Y, validate its assumed attention-noise models, or account for finite-sample approximation and the paper's selective-label classification procedure.

The repeated description of the approach as annotation-free is overstated. Although spatial labels are generated internally, training still depends on 152K curated, externally annotated question-image pairs from GQA and OCR-VQA; even the 10K setting uses such supervision.

Results lack repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests, which is relevant because several improvements outside DocVQA, TextVQA, and V-Star are small and hyperparameters were selected empirically on the evaluated tasks.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: improving fine-grained MLLM perception without uniformly processing high-resolution images.
SD-RPN is intuitive and potentially useful: it distills response-conditioned attention into a small proposal module that runs before answer generation.
The reported gains are substantial across several OCR, document, spatial-reasoning, and high-resolution benchmarks, and the method is tested on two model families and multiple scales.
The component ablations cover attention prediction, label assignment, sink-token removal, upscaling strategy, backbone depth, RPN depth, and training-set size.
Training appears economical, and the 10K-sample results suggest promising data efficiency.
weaknesses: The experimental model-selection protocol threatens the validity of the main results. The paper states that model-specific layers were chosen through ablations, while those ablations use evaluation benchmarks including OCRBench test and V-Star. Upscaling strategy, RPN depth, and other design choices are likewise selected on these benchmarks, with no separate validation protocol described. This creates substantial risk of test-set tuning.

The comparison set is too narrow for the broad claims. Only S2 and ViCrop are compared on LLaVA, and neither is reported for DeepSeek-VL. There are no comparisons with several relevant trained RoI/token-selection approaches discussed in the paper, recent high-resolution MLLMs, a compute-matched random or saliency crop, or an oracle crop/full-resolution upper bound.

The claimed localization improvement is not directly evaluated. No bounding-box IoU, pointing-game accuracy, recall, crop coverage, selected-area distribution, or quantitative pseudo-label quality is reported. Figure 3 provides an incomplete analysis without clear sample size or uncertainty, while the qualitative examples are explicitly cherry-picked.

The efficiency evidence is incomplete. Only relative end-to-end throughput is given, without absolute latency, batch size, decoding length/settings, visual-token counts, crop-area statistics, memory use, or separate timing of proposal and second-stage processing. Consequently, the stated 1.5x speedup of the RoI prediction stage is not established by the presented tables.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The code link is blank, and essential values such as the sink-norm threshold, inference threshold, Gaussian-filter parameters, crop resizing rules, maximum number of regions/tokens, and detailed evaluation and decoding settings are omitted.

The appendix's theoretical argument is largely tautological: defining h*(X)=E[A|X] makes its MSE relative to itself zero. This only shows that conditional expectation denoises attention under assumed noise models; it does not establish improved estimation of the latent foreground Y, justify those assumptions for transformer attention, or prove that a finite learned RPN and the proposed label assignment improve localization.

Calling the method annotation-free is overstated. Although it avoids bounding-box labels and uses self-generated answers, training still relies on 152K curated image-question pairs from GQA and OCR-VQA. The claim should be narrowed to localization-annotation-free.

Several results are less uniformly favorable than the presentation suggests: gains on POPE and some HR-Bench submetrics are small or negative relative to competing methods, and improvements are reported against the low-resolution baseline rather than consistently against the strongest comparator. No confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or significance tests are provided.

The use of benchmark-specific empirical choices and datasets closely aligned with the target domains leaves cross-domain generalization insufficiently demonstrated. Potential image/source overlap between training and evaluation collections is also not analyzed.

The empirical gains are substantial and consistent across diverse document, OCR, vision-centric, and high-resolution benchmarks; the method also transfers across LLaVA-1.5 and DeepSeek-VL model sizes.
The component ablations are informative: label assignment, sink-token removal, masking, backbone depth, RPN depth, and training-set size are each examined.
Training requires only a lightweight three-layer RPN over a frozen backbone, and the 10K-sample results provide credible evidence of data efficiency.
The presentation is generally clear, with useful architectural diagrams, an explicit training algorithm, and qualitative examples supporting the proposed localization behavior.
weaknesses: The comparison set is too narrow for a top-tier paper: it includes only S2 and ViCrop and omits several training-based RoI, adaptive-resolution, token-selection, and crop-selection approaches discussed in the paper. Matched-compute, random-crop, confidence-based crop, and oracle-region controls are also absent.

The paper never directly evaluates RoI quality using localization metrics such as recall, pointing accuracy, or IoU. Consequently, the central claim that denoising produces higher-quality localization is supported only indirectly through downstream VQA accuracy and selected qualitative examples.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The displayed code link is empty, while essential details—including the sink threshold, Gaussian parameters, final mask threshold, crop resizing, handling or limits of connected components, token budget, and precise throughput protocol—are unspecified.

Efficiency evidence is limited to relative throughput on one GPU, without absolute latency, memory, FLOPs, visual-token counts, or a breakdown of proposal, crop encoding, and generation costs. The claimed 1.5x faster RoI prediction is not separately substantiated by the reported end-to-end measurements.

The term “annotation-free” is overstated because training still relies on questions drawn from annotated GQA and OCR-VQA datasets; the method is more accurately region-annotation-free. Potential overlap or distribution relationships between training and evaluation datasets are not analyzed.

The theoretical appendix is largely tautological: defining the target as E[A|X] makes its MSE against itself zero, but this does not establish improvement with respect to the latent foreground variable, nor account for finite-sample approximation error or the actual continuous, selectively thresholded labels.

The core technique combines attention thresholding, sink removal, pseudo-labeling, and a small initialized prediction head. This is sensible and effective, but the conceptual novelty is moderate, and validation on stronger contemporary MLLMs would be needed to establish broader significance.

strengths: The paper identifies an important practical problem: improving fine-grained MLLM perception without uniformly processing high-resolution images or requiring spatial annotations.

SD-RPN is a sensible and useful design: it denoises response-to-image attention, learns a lightweight region predictor from pseudo-labels, and uses intermediate MLLM features to reduce localization overhead.

The downstream evaluation is unusually broad, covering six model configurations from three MLLM families and document/OCR, visual-search, hallucination, and high-resolution benchmarks. The improvements are generally large and consistent.

The component, backbone-depth, RPN-depth, data-size, smoothing, and threshold ablations provide useful evidence for several design decisions. Results with only 10K training samples also suggest promising data efficiency.

The paper includes throughput measurements, comparisons with an external grounding model, qualitative successes, and an informative failure analysis. The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/84f66cb7e40747548d3cd915332d4526/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The evaluation appears to use target benchmarks for model selection. The backbone depth is selected using OCRBench, TextVQA, POPE, and V-Star results, and the foreground/background thresholds are optimized on the same benchmarks. OCRBench is explicitly a test split. No separate validation protocol is described, and layer choices for the other architectures are merely said to be selected empirically. This compromises the strength of the reported evaluation.

The central claim of more precise localization is evaluated almost entirely through downstream QA accuracy. There is no systematic bounding-box, pointing-game, recall-at-area, or crop-coverage evaluation comparing the learned RPN with raw attention, ViCrop, and external grounders. Consequently, accuracy gains could partly arise from changes in token allocation or image preprocessing rather than improved localization.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important settings are missing or insufficiently specified, including the numerical sink-token norm threshold, Gaussian kernel parameters, inference threshold, connected-component filtering, crop enlargement/resizing, maximum number of crops/tokens, response-generation settings, and whether computation from the partial first pass is cached or recomputed.

The efficiency evidence is not fully controlled. Relative throughput is reported without a precise measurement protocol, latency decomposition, memory usage, FLOPs, generated-answer length controls, or matched visual-token budgets. Comparisons with Thyme and DeepEyes lack measured runtime, while the claim of substantially lower cost is therefore only partially supported.

Appendix F overstates its theoretical result. It defines the target signal as h*(X)=E[A|X] and then trivially shows that h* has zero error relative to itself. This establishes conditional averaging of attention under assumed noise models, not better localization relative to the latent foreground Y. It also does not analyze the paper's actual selective pseudo-label classification procedure, finite data, or model misspecification.

Some quantitative reporting is inconsistent. For example, Table 3 reports OCRBench 32.8 versus a 31.4 baseline as a +2.4 gain, although the difference is +1.4; its displayed average improvements for rows 1 and 2 also do not match the tabulated values. Such errors weaken confidence in result auditing.

The abstract's claim that 10K samples produce over 10% absolute improvements on DocVQA, TextVQA, and V-Star is not fully substantiated: the 10K ablation reports TextVQA and V-Star but not DocVQA. The strongest main results instead use 152K samples.

Novelty is moderate rather than compelling: the approach combines known attention-based localization, sink-token suppression, selective pseudo-labeling, and a small initialized transformer head. The paper needs cleaner held-out model selection and direct localization evidence to demonstrate that this combination clears the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important practical problem: improving fine-grained MLLM perception without uniformly processing images at high resolution. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/6274610568b1495e8f9a6df1dcb55a3d/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The proposed combination of attention denoising, selective pseudo-label assignment, and a lightweight predictor attached to intermediate MLLM layers is technically plausible and practically motivated.

The experiments cover multiple model families and several OCR, document, visual-search, hallucination, and high-resolution benchmarks, with often substantial improvements over the corresponding unmodified models.
The component, backbone-depth, RPN-depth, data-size, threshold, and smoothing ablations provide useful evidence about the proposed design. The inclusion of failure cases is also welcome.
The method appears relatively inexpensive to train, and the reported accuracy-throughput curves suggest that selective cropping can outperform merely increasing Qwen2.5-VL's input resolution.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol raises a serious test-set-tuning concern. Key thresholds and architectural choices are selected using performance on OCRBench test, V-Star, and other eventual evaluation benchmarks. Figure 3 also uses a TextVQA subset with ground-truth boxes to motivate the foreground threshold. No separate validation protocol is documented, so the reported generalization evidence may be optimistically biased.

The comparisons do not cleanly isolate the proposed contribution. SD-RPN receives up to 152K additional task-domain question-image samples, whereas prominent comparisons are training-free or have different training recipes. Most alternative methods are evaluated only for LLaVA, while DeepSeek-VL is compared almost exclusively with its own baseline and the Qwen comparisons are incomplete. Equal-data, equal-token-budget, and equal-compute controls are missing.

Calling the method annotation-free is overstated: it depends on 152K questions drawn from annotated VQA datasets, even if their answers are not used. The abstract further foregrounds training with only 10K samples, although the main results use 152K, and the claimed greater-than-10-point 10K improvement on DocVQA is not actually reported in the data-size ablation.

The central claim of more precise localization is never evaluated directly with IoU, pointing accuracy, proposal recall, or another localization metric. Downstream VQA gains cannot establish that the learned RPN is more spatially accurate than raw attention, particularly because cropping also changes resolution and token allocation.

The theoretical appendix is largely tautological. It defines the target signal as E[A|X] and then observes that this conditional expectation has lower error with respect to itself than a noisy sample A. The assumed affine relationship between attention and the latent foreground label is neither justified nor tested, and the analysis does not prove that a finite learned predictor improves true localization.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the extensive appendix. The code link is empty, and important details such as the sink-norm threshold, inference threshold, Gaussian parameters, crop expansion and resizing rules, connected-component handling, maximum crop/token budget, and several model-specific choices are absent.

The efficiency evidence is incomplete. Relative throughput is not precisely defined, there are no memory or FLOP measurements, and pseudo-label-generation cost is omitted. The claim that the RPN reuses computation the MLLM must perform anyway is also questionable for a two-stage procedure that runs an additional partial pass before the final augmented-context pass.

Results are presented as single numbers without multiple runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This matters for small gains on POPE, ChartQA, and several Qwen benchmarks and for the non-monotonic data-size and backbone-depth ablations.

Overall, the idea is promising and the headline gains are notable, but evaluation leakage risks, unfair or incomplete controls, unsupported localization and annotation-free claims, and missing reproducibility details prevent the work from meeting the evidentiary standard of a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The manuscript presents a clear and practically relevant contribution: SD-RPN distills an MLLM's response-conditioned attention into a lightweight RoI predictor, avoiding external region annotations and autoregressive localization at inference. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/4e0db79225e54a60badee684d2538a3a/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The empirical results are strong and broad: improvements are demonstrated on document/OCR, general visual, and high-resolution benchmarks across LLaVA-1.5, DeepSeek-VL, and Qwen2.5-VL model families.

The method offers a compelling accuracy-efficiency trade-off. It substantially outperforms direct attention-based cropping and is faster than ViCrop and an external Grounding-DINO-based pipeline, while the resolution-scaling experiment supports its advantage over simply increasing visual-token counts.

The ablations meaningfully isolate label assignment, sink-token removal, upscaling strategy, backbone depth, RPN depth, training-set size, smoothing, and foreground/background thresholds. The strong results with only 10K training examples are especially encouraging.
The paper is generally clear and includes useful qualitative successes, explicit failure cases, algorithmic pseudocode, training hyperparameters, and an analysis of common attention-noise sources.
weaknesses: The central 'annotation-free' description is somewhat overstated: although no RoI annotations are used, training still relies on 152K human-curated image-question pairs from GQA and OCR-VQA. The distinction between region-annotation-free and fully annotation-free learning should be stated precisely.

Some hyperparameters appear selected using the same benchmarks on which final performance is reported. In particular, Table 5 optimizes thresholds directly over OCRBench, TextVQA, POPE, and V-Star, while model-specific layers are also empirically selected without a clearly identified validation protocol. This creates a risk of benchmark overfitting and weakens the generalization claim.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The promised code URL is blank, and important details such as the sink-token norm threshold, Gaussian-filter parameters, inference threshold, crop resizing, connected-component rules, prompt/decoding settings, and precise throughput protocol are missing or insufficiently specified.

The theoretical section is weak: it defines the ideal predictor as the conditional expectation and then observes that this ideal has zero error relative to itself. This does not establish that the learned finite-sample RPN improves on raw attention, nor does it justify the selective pseudo-labeling procedure under realistic, feature-dependent noise.

The efficiency discussion occasionally overstates computation reuse. RoI prediction still requires an additional partial MLLM pass before the augmented final pass; the paper should clarify exactly what activations are reused and report end-to-end latency, memory, FLOPs, token counts, and batch conditions consistently for all major comparisons.

Results are reported without multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance estimates. Several gains on the strongest Qwen baseline are modest, so uncertainty would be useful. Comparisons are also uneven across model families, with S2/ViCrop mainly tested for LLaVA and recent methods largely taken from reported numbers.

The method is inherently limited when the answer depends on several distant regions, precise spatial relations, or an RoI missed during the first stage. The failure analysis acknowledges these cases, but their frequency and the impact of fallback strategies are not quantified.
